short: A century in which one authority over Eurasia made the Silk Road safe end to end.
full:
With the steppe under a single family, the overland routes between China and the Mediterranean became passable for the first time in centuries. Merchants travelled under Mongol protection along the yam roads, taxed at predictable rates; the Florentine Francesco Pegolotti wrote around 1340 that the road to Cathay was perfectly safe by day or night. Franciscan friars reached Karakorum, Marco Polo's family reached Dadu, and the Mongol ilkhans corresponded with the kings of England and France.

What moved was not only silk. Persian astronomers worked at Chinese observatories and Chinese medicine reached Tabriz; Rashid al-Din compiled a history using informants from both ends of the continent. Gunpowder, the blast furnace, printing and the counterweight trebuchet all spread along these routes. So did Yersinia pestis: the plague that reached Caffa in 1346 and Europe the following year travelled the same corridors. The peace ended with them, as the khanates fell into civil war, the Ilkhanate dissolved in 1335 and the Yuan lost China in 1368.
